## Appendix C <br> Lie Groups

In most cases of relevance for physics, infinite-dimensional groups are used. Such a group is called a Lie group G if

(i) the elements $\mathrm{g} \in \mathrm{G}$ form an (analytic) manifold,
(ii) the mapping $\mathrm{G} \times \mathrm{G} \rightarrow \mathrm{G}$ originating from the pointwise multiplication $\left(\mathrm{g}_{1}, \mathrm{~g}_{2}\right) \rightarrow \mathrm{g}_{1} \mathrm{~g}_{2}^{-1}$ of (group) elements is analytic as well.

The most general example is given by $\mathrm{G}=\mathrm{GL}(\mathrm{N}, \mathbb{C})$, i.e., by the general linear group of complex $\mathrm{N} \times \mathrm{N}$ matrices.

The tangent space $\mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{e}}(\mathrm{G})$ attached to the unit element $\mathrm{e} \in \mathrm{G}$ of the group possesses the structure of a vector space of dimension $\mathrm{K}=\operatorname{dim} \mathrm{G}$, and as such is isomorphic to the Lie algebra of $\mathfrak{g}$ of G (KN I., p. 38). Let $\xi=\left\{\xi^{\mathrm{j}}, \mathrm{j}=1, \ldots, \mathrm{~K}\right\}$ be an appropriate parametrization of G. Then the matrices

$$
I_{j}:=\left.\frac{\partial g(\xi)}{\partial \xi^{j}}\right|_{g=e} \in T_{e}(G) \approx \mathfrak{g}
$$

are the infinitesimal generators of G. Viewed oppositely, the transition from the Lie algebra $\mathfrak{g}$ to the group G is mediated by the exponential mapping

$$
\exp : \mathfrak{g} \rightarrow G \ni g=\exp \left(\iota \xi^{j} I_{j}\right)
$$

in terms of matrices. The vector space spanned by the infinitesimal generators is turned into the corresponding Lie algebra by prescribing the commutation relations

$$
\left[I_{i}, I_{j}\right]=c_{i j}{ }^{k} I_{k} .
$$

Here the real structure constants $\mathrm{c}_{\mathrm{ij}}^{\mathrm{k}}$ are characteristic of the group G . They are always antisymmetric

$$
c_{i j}^{k}=-c_{j i}^{k}
$$

with respect to the first two indices. Moreover, they satisfy the cyclic Jacobi identity

$$
3 c_{[i \mid s}{ }^{p} c_{\mid j k]}{ }^{s}:=c_{i s}{ }^{p} c_{j k}{ }^{s}+c_{j s}{ }^{p} c_{k i}{ }^{s}+c_{k s}{ }^{p} c_{i j}{ }^{s} \equiv 0 .
$$

As a result, the Lie product

$$
[\mathrm{AB}]:=\mathrm{A}^{\mathrm{i}} \mathrm{~B}^{\mathrm{j}} \mathrm{c}_{\mathrm{ij}}^{\mathrm{k}} \mathrm{I}_{\mathrm{k}} .
$$

defined for generic Lie-algebra-valued vectors $\mathrm{A}=\mathrm{A}^{\mathrm{i}} \mathrm{I}_{\mathrm{i}}$ and $\mathrm{B}=\mathrm{B}^{\mathrm{j}} \mathrm{I}_{\mathrm{j}}$ is linear and antisymmetric. Moreover, it satisfies the Jacobi identity, as required.

For applications in physics it is not the group itself, but more often the group's linear representations that are considered. The latter are derived from a Lie homomorphism $\rho: \mathrm{G} \rightarrow \mathrm{GL}(\mathrm{N}, \mathbb{C})$, i.e., from an injective, continuous, and open mapping into the general group of complex matrices. This homomorphism inherits the matrix multiplication

$$
\rho_{A}^{C}\left(g_{1}\right) \rho_{C}^{B}\left(g_{2}\right)=\rho_{A}^{B}\left(g_{1} g_{2}\right)
$$

from the multiplication rûle of the group in question. The "derived" homomorphism generates a representation of the Lie algebra via

$$
[A, B] \longrightarrow \rho([A, B])=[\rho(A), \rho(B)] .
$$

An example of prime importance is the adjoint representation

$$
\operatorname{Ad} A(B):=[A, B] ; \quad A, B \in \mathfrak{g},
$$

which reads explicitly, with regard to the basis $\mathrm{I}_{\mathrm{j}}$,

$$
(\operatorname{Ad} A)_{j}{ }^{k}=c_{i j}{ }^{k} A^{i} .
$$

With the aid of the trace operation Tr, a scalar product

$$
(A, B):=\operatorname{Tr}(\operatorname{Ad} A \operatorname{Ad} B)=c_{\iota k}^{i} c_{s i}^{k} A^{\iota} B^{s}=: \stackrel{\circ}{g}_{\iota s} A^{\iota} B^{s}
$$

may be introduced that is determined by the Cartan-Killing metric $\stackrel{\circ}{g}_{l s}$ of the Lie algebra. This scalar product is invariant with respect to the group of automorphisms of $\mathfrak{g}$. In the case of the Lie algebra $\mathfrak{g l}(\mathrm{N}, \mathbb{C})$ of the general linear group, this product can be written as follows:

$$
(A, B)=2 N \operatorname{Tr}(A B)-2 \operatorname{Tr}(A) \operatorname{Tr}(B)
$$

Barut \& Rączka 1980, p. 15). For the special groups that by definition satisfy $\operatorname{det} \mathrm{G}=1$, the last term vanishes. This is a consequence of the matrix identity det $\mathrm{G}=\exp ^{\mathrm{Trg}}$. The scalar product (C.12) is nondegenerate if and only if G is semisimple, i.e., if G does not contain an abelian invariant subgroup. A closer analysis (Helgason 1962) of the Cartan-Killing metric

$$
\stackrel{\circ}{g}_{l m}:=c_{l k}{ }^{i} c_{m i}{ }^{k}
$$

reveals that every simple Lie group, regarded as a manifold, corresponds either to a Riemannian manifold or a pseudo-Riemannian manifold. This may indicate why (C.13) can also be regarded as the metric of the group manifold.

The group that is frequently discussed in connection with the quark model (Gell-Mann \& Ne'eman 1964; Kokkedee 1969) is the simple group SU(N) or its Lie algebra. In terms of a real parametrization $\xi^{\mathrm{j}}$, an arbitrary group element is generated by

$$
g=\exp ^{\left(-\frac{i}{2} \xi^{j} \lambda_{j}\right)} \in S U(N), j=1, \ldots, N^{2}-1 .
$$

Here the $\lambda_{\mathrm{j}}$ denote the generalized Gell-Mann matrices, which are Hermitian and trace-free. Their commutation and anticommutation relations are specified by

$$
\begin{aligned}
{\left[\lambda_{i}, \lambda_{j}\right] } & =2 i \mathrm{f}_{i j}^{k} \lambda_{k} \quad\left(c_{i j}^{k}=2 i f_{i g}^{k}\right), \\
\left\{\lambda_{i}, \lambda_{j}\right\}_{+} & =\frac{4}{N} \delta_{i j}+2 d_{i j}^{k} \lambda_{k} .
\end{aligned}
$$

It is a consequence of these relations that the product of two of such matrices can always be written in the following form:

$$
\lambda_{i} \lambda_{j}=\frac{2}{N} \delta_{i j}+\left(d_{i j}^{k}+i f_{i j}^{k}\right) \lambda_{k} .
$$

In these formulas, it is understood that the $\lambda$-matrices are normalized according to

$$
\operatorname{Tr}\left(\lambda_{i} \lambda_{j}\right)=2 \delta_{i j} .
$$
